https://hungarytoday.hu/let-the-looting-.text: Let the Looting Begin: Far Left Soros NGOs to Nominate Members of Controversial “Asset Recovery Office” It may soon become clear who will take the helm of the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office (NVVH), which has been dubbed the “new Stasi” in reference to the notorious East German secret police. Three well-known organizations will assist TISZA officials in making a decision, Magyar Nemzet reported. The chair of the Parliament’s Justice Committee, István Hantosi (TISZA) shared the schedule on Sunday, noting that the selection process will reach its most critical phase this week after the applications received for the positions of chair and vice chair of the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office (NVVH) have been evaluated. On Monday, he announced that only three candidates—Miklós Ligeti, Anna Róza Unger, and Dávid Jancsics—remain in the running for the presidency of the NVVH. The finalists come from diverse professional backgrounds. Miklós Ligeti is a lawyer and the legal director of Transparency International Hungary, a self-declared “anti-corruption” organization linked to the Soros network. Anna Róza Unger is a political scientist and associate professor at the Faculty of Social Sciences at Eötvös Loránd University. Her research focuses on direct democracy, electoral systems, and political financing. In recent years, she has also contributed to programs on the Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, a liberal-leaning international broadcaster, and the radical left-leaning Partizán . Dávid Jancsics is a sociologist and “corruption researcher” who lives and works in the United States, he is currently a professor at San Diego State University. “To ensure genuine public oversight and professional safeguards, we consider the involvement of civil society to be crucial. The invited civil society organizations directly help us make the best possible decision through their expertise, independent perspectives, and professional knowledge, and their presence ensures the highest level of transparency toward the public,” Hantosi explained. He then revealed which three civil society organizations will consult with them prior to the selection process: the Hungarian Civil Liberties Union (TASZ), the Hungarian Helsinki Committee, and the nonprofit organization K-Monitor. All three are strongly left-leaning NGOs with diverse ties to the Soros network, known for their long track-record of attacking the previous conservative government of Viktor Orbán. Hantosi also emphasized that Prime Minister Péter Magyar will not have the right to veto the selection process. The FIDESZ parliamentary group had previously announced that it would not participate in the nomination and selection of NVVH leaders because it considers the regulations governing the agency to be unconstitutional in several respects. Gábor Szűcs, a FIDESZ member of parliament, also reaffirmed the party’s position in a Facebook post on Monday. He stated that FIDESZ will appeal to the Constitutional Court regarding the “the secret police law,” since “the entire organization is merely a tool of Péter Magyar’s autocracy,” whose goal is to settle political scores with his opponents. The main criticism of the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office is that it creates a “super-agency” unprecedented in the Hungarian legal system. Since the agency is to be granted hybrid powers—combining administrative, investigative, and prosecutorial (prosecutor’s office) authorities—the proposal is facing sharp criticism from multiple quarters. János Bóka, the FIDESZ parliamentary group leader, had particularly harsh words . “If you think you can turn to another authority to challenge the arbitrariness or abuses of the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office, you are sorely mistaken. The agency can take over any proceeding at any time, and there is no legal remedy against this decision,” the politician warned. János Bóka drew a historical comparison to the notorious communist state security agency, the ÁVH. Even that agency, he said, did not possess “as much power on paper” as is now being granted to the new agency. Since this is not formally a classic administrative proceeding, those affected have neither the right to an attorney nor to general judicial protection, said the FIDESZ politician. Legal experts and constitutional analysts also expressed concerns regarding the rule of law. The broad, horizontal powers of the agency were particularly criticized. The fact that the agency may, in certain cases, replace the regular public prosecutor’s office and bring charges independently undermines the principle of the separation of powers and violates the public prosecutor’s traditional monopoly on prosecution. World ABC News LONDON -- President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff hailed what he described as "very meaningful discussions" regarding the Ukraine-Russia war, saying the talks in Kyiv Sunday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy were "substantive [and] important." Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, arrived in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv on Sunday in a renewed White House push for progress on ending Russia's full-scale invasion of its neighbor, now in its fifth year. "President Trump asked us to convey his personal regards to you and to the people of Ukraine," Kushner told Zelenskyy in comments before reporters, adding that Trump "wanted us to convey that he sees this as a very, very hard and complex problem, but it's a very worthy problem worth solving." He added that Trump was committed not only to ending the conflict, but also to securing a lasting peace that would enable Ukraine "to build itself into the great nation that they [Ukraine] have the fullest potential to achieve." Zelenskyy thanked the United States for its continued support and expressed gratitude to Trump for "allowing the American group to be here in Ukraine today." "After the meetings in the Russian Federation, it was very important for us to have President Trump's chief negotiators in Ukraine today," Zelenskyy said. The U.S. delegation traveled to Ukraine following talks in Moscow on Saturday, during which Witkoff and Kushner sat down with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss what a White House official told ABC News were "substantive plans for next steps" on the path toward a peace deal, despite few signs peace is any closer. The visit to Kyiv by Witkoff and Kushner is their first during the full-scale invasion. The pair have visited Russia several times during the conflict. They arrived from Poland by train before being welcomed by President Zelenskyy outside the historic Saint Sophia Cathedral in the center of the capital. Zelenskyy embraced the two the men before leading them inside the cathedral. Prior to their arrival, Zelenskyy wrote in a post on X that he had met with Ukraine's negotiating team and was expecting a "substantive conversation" with the U.S. envoys. "Ukraine has always been and will remain constructive. We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer. Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A dignified character of the postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are ready," he wrote in a post to X. The national security advisers of France, Germany and the U.K. were among senior European officials who also traveled to Kyiv to take part in Sunday's talks. A source told ABC News the American delegation was serious about the meetings in Moscow and Kyiv, adding that the visits are "not just for show." According to the source, the American side wants to end the war before winter, while Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Zelenskyy's office, believes this will not be possible and that Russia will only be genuinely ready for negotiations in the spring or summer 2027. The American negotiating pair spent more than three hours with Putin in the Kremlin on Saturday, with U.S. and Russian officials both praising the discussions. But Putin afterward gave no sign of compromise. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told the state-run Tass news agency that Putin told Witkoff and Kushner that it was necessary to eliminate "all root causes of the Ukrainian conflict," a phrase routinely used by officials in Moscow hinting at maximalist Russian demands that Ukraine be forced to accept neutrality, cut down its military and abandon any NATO aspirations. Putin also "noted the successes of Russian forces" in the ongoing war effort "and expressed confidence in achieving its goals," Ushakov said. Most experts believe Putin's position in recent weeks has only hardened, with signs he believes Russia is winning the war and is more determined to use military force to try to force concessions from Kyiv, including by targeting its energy system this winter. In the last two weeks, Russia has significantly intensified its air attacks on Kyiv, using jet-powered drones to relentlessly terrorize the capital. At the start of Saturday's meeting, Witkoff thanked Putin for hosting the American delegation and noted the "incredible" stories and memories that he, Kushner, Ushakov and Russian Direct Investment Fund CEO Kirill Dmitriev will have when they retire. "Yours will be right at the top of it all," Witkoff said. Witkoff also conveyed Trump's best wishes and thanked Putin on behalf of the Gilman family for helping secure the return of Rob Gilman. Putin said that the credit belonged to Trump. A White House official told ABC News that Kushner and Witkoff were joined by officials from the National Security Council, State Department and Treasury Department during the discussions on "proposals to bring peace to this conflict." Witkoff further thanked Putin for supporting what he described as a temporary "no-shoot" arrangement around Kyiv and Moscow, which allowed the American delegation to travel safely to and from Russia. Putin and Zelenskyy have both publicly said they will not strike each other's capitals during the American delegations visits. While no Russian strikes struck Kyiv overnight Saturday, drones were reported to have targeted the nearby city of Boryspil. Russian strikes continued in the rest of Ukraine. The Kremlin meeting did little to encourage Ukrainians, Oleksandr Merezhko -- a member of the Ukrainian parliament and the chair of the body's foreign affairs committee -- told ABC News on Sunday. "We are expecting Trump's envoy but I don't have any hopes at all," he said from Kyiv. This is something that Trump doesn't understand -- Putin believes that there is no way back for him. He has committed so many crimes that, as he believes, he can save his skin only if Ukraine capitulates." Merezhko said he was among those skeptical of Witkof and Kushner's ability to chart a path to a settlement, describing the pair as "amateurs without necessary knowledge and experience." Both Russia and Ukraine continued long-range overnight strikes. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 108 drones and an unspecified number of cruise missiles into the country overnight into Sunday morning. Air defenses downed 82 drones and six cruise missiles, the air force said, with impacts reported across 11 locations. Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported at least one attack in the Kyiv region, where a Russian strike caused a "large-scale fire" at an infrastructure facility. Russia's Defense Ministry, meanwhile, said its forces downed 258 Ukrainian drones overnight, with craft reported shot down over 14 Russian regions, occupied Crimea, the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov. https://www.dw.com/en/why-russia-s-arres.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OanL Journalist Yuki Imai seen being taken into custody by Russian security agents Image: Russian Federal Security Service/TASS/picture alliance Advertisement Japanese Foreign Ministry officials were in Moscow this week in an attempt to contact a journalist arrested in Russia's far east on allegations of spying . Journalist Yuki Imai was arrested on October 14 by Russia's FSB security service in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on Sakhalin Island. Televised footage of the arrest showed FSB officers barging into his hotel room as he slept. The correspondent for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper was accused of attempting to obtain information on soldiers in the region, which is near the Kiril islands, a geopolitical sore spot in Russia - Japan relations. Russian authorities quickly transferred him to Lefortovo Prison in Moscow, where a court ordered him to be held in pretrial detention until at least December 12. If convicted, 34-year-old Imai faces up to 20 years in jail, according to the International Federation of Journalists, which has called for his immediate release. Officials from the Japanese embassy in Moscow have been denied access to Imai. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has condemned the arrest and dismissed the claim that Imai was a spy. Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev said Imai had been caught "red-handed," the official TASS news agency reported. Nozdrev has claimed that Japanese intelligence agencies use journalists to collect classified information with the goal of "undermining Russia's security and defense capability." Russia accuses journalists of being 'spies' Yoji Gomi, a veteran journalist and author who has reported from across Asia, told DW that Japanese journalists may occasionally meet with diplomats in the course of their work and "share thoughts and impressions." However, he rejects the idea that reporters are paid spies. "One-party nations often see foreign correspondents as spies because that is exactly what they use their journalists for," he said. "I can completely see how the Russians decided that Imai was a spy, as it is how they operate, plus he was in a sensitive part of Russia where there are lots of North Korean laborers that they want to keep quiet," Gomi added. Japan condemns Putin visit to disputed Kuril Islands To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Stephen Nagy, a professor of international relations at Tokyo's International Christian University, told DW that Russia might see Imai as a bargaining chip it can use to exchange for nationals detained overseas. Nagy doubts that Japan will give in to pressure. "They are going to resist because it means that Russia, or any other country, can then just seize a Japanese national, put them on trial for espionage and demand the release of one of their people," he said. "It would set a dangerous precedent," he added. The arrest comes after a member of the Russia-linked hacking group Qilin was arrested in Japan and extradited to Germany to face charges in connection with a 2024 cyberattack on a logistics center. The last time a journalist was arrested in Russia was in 2019 for "attempting to obtain classified information about Russia's military potential in the Far East," Russia's Interfax news agency reported. However, in this case, the journalist was quickly released. Imai's case is perhaps the most serious since 2023, when Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich was arrested in Russia and sentenced to 16 years in a penal colony before being released in a prisoner exchange with Western countries in 2024. Russia has previously arrested foreign journalists for prisoner exchanges. US reporter Evan Gershkovich is seen here in a Moscow court. Image: Dmitry Serebryakov/AP/picture alliance Strained Japan-Russia ties Imai's arrest is the latest in a series of incidents that have sent bilateral relations into a tailspin . Nagy said Imai's seizure was designed to put pressure on Tokyo. He added this is part of a coordinated approach with China to isolate Japan at a time when the US is preoccupied with domestic issues and the conflict in the Middle East. "Moscow and Beijing are coordinating to create the image that Japan is not a reformed member of the international community but still the military state of the 1930s and that it poses a threat to stability in the Indo-Pacific region," Nagy said. "This is all designed to smear Japan's efforts to lead diplomacy in the region at a time when the US is perhaps distracted," he said. "And it does not even matter much that it is not true; they will just continue to repeat the claim to discredit and weaken Tokyo." Decadeslong row over disputed islands Tadashi Anno, a professor of politics at Tokyo's Sophia University, told DW that he believes Japan had been working hard to maintain a stable relationship with Russia, even after Tokyo joined international condemnation of the invasion of Ukraine . Anno said Russia's timing in turning up the heat on Japan was puzzling. "Japan condemned the invasion of Ukraine in 2022 because it was a fundamental violation of international law, but Russia is only now pushing back hard," he said. At the center of deteriorating ties is a territorial dispute about a chain of islands off the far north of Japan that were seized by Soviet forces after Japan's surrender in World War II. There had been hopes in the past in Tokyo that a concerted diplomatic effort could be sufficient to convince Russia to return the islands — known as the Northern Territories in Japan and the Southern Kurils by Russia — to Japanese sovereignty. That campaign has faltered in the past couple of years, and was further dented when Japan announced in the spring that it would be joining the NATO initiative to provide nonlethal assistance to Kyiv. In August, President Vladimir Putin visited the disputed islands , becoming only the second Russian leader to do so. Earlier this month, a delegation of Chinese businesspeople was welcomed on one of the islands, and talks are underway on the possibility of economic cooperation.
